In contrast to these static measures, Treynor and
Mazuy (1966) were among the ﬁrst to propose a
dynamic measure of active management. To pick
up market-timing skills, Treynor and Mazuy (1966)
augmented the linear framework of (1) with a
quadratic term (Rmt −Rf )2. Formally, this is still a
contemporaneous regression, hence its parameters
do not involve any time-series properties, but the
motivation—to detect asymmetries in up and down
markets—is distinctly dynamic.
In a recent comment on the fundamental index-
ation approach of Arnott et al. (2005), Treynor
(2005) does focus on the covariance between port-
folio weights and returns, but only in the speciﬁc
context of explaining the potential improvements of
fundamental indexation over market-capitalization
weights. The AP decomposition described in this
paper provides a considerably more general frame-
work for thinking about the beneﬁts and costs of
any indexation algorithm.
A more explicit measure of market-timing skill is
given by Merton (1981), Henriksson and Merton
(1981), and Henriksson (1984), who showed that
perfect market-timing is equivalent to a buy-and-
hold investment in the market that is fully protected
by put options on the market with a riskless-rate
strike. Imperfect market-timing skill may then be
modeled as a partially insured investment in the
market. Although this measure may also seem like
a static one because it involves parameters at a
single point in time of the multivariate distribution
of market returns and corresponding put-option
prices, it is, in fact, dynamic due to the multi-
period nature of options prices.2 In other words, the
dynamics of market-timing have been compressed
into the put-option price, which is then used as
the “numeraire” for market-timing skill in Merton’s
(1981) framework.
Two other related studies are by Brinson et al.
(1986) and Brinson et al. (1991), in which they
decompose the realized return of a portfolio into
three components: a benchmark return, the return
from asset allocation (measured by the product
of returns and the deviations of the portfolio’s
asset-class weights from the benchmark’s asset-
class weights), and the return of security selection
(measured by the product of returns and the devi-
ations of individual portfolio weights from the
benchmark’s portfolio weights within each asset
class):
Rpt = Rbt + Rat + Rst.
(6)
Although this decomposition seems to be simi-
lar in spirit to the one proposed in this paper,
there is an important difference: the deﬁnitions of
“security selection” and “asset allocation” in Brin-
son et al. (1986) are measures deﬁned with respect
to a benchmark, not time-series measures of a
manager’s forecast power in each of these cate-
gories. However, by taking expectations of (6) and
using the decomposition described in Section 3,
it is possible to extend the framework of Brinson
et al. (1986) to yield measures of forecast power
for security-selection and asset-allocation decisions
separately. Another difference between (6) and
the approach described in this paper is the criti-
cal dependence of (6) on the benchmark, which
may be appropriate for managers whose invest-
ment mandates specify such benchmarks explicitly,
